name: Glenwood Gardens (now Canyon Vista Apartments)
award: 2024 Federal 4% and state housing tax credits (Round Two)
headline: Cohen-Esrey plans Glenwood Gardens, renamed Canyon Vista Apartments, 80 all-electric income-restricted apartments for households at 20% to 80% AMI on about four acres at 51993 Highway 6 in West Glenwood Springs, with eight Garfield County Housing Authority project-based vouchers; it won 2024 Round Two federal 4% and accelerated state credits with $25.13M of CHFA bonds but had not broken ground as of October 2026.
why_it_matters: CHFA calls it the first new-construction family development in Glenwood Springs since 2011 and the area's first with 20% AMI units, and it shows how far a mountain-town 4% deal has to stack local money: about $3.8M of city lodging-tax funds, county bond cap and a Proposition 123 loan after federal sustainability money fell away.

status.label: Credits awarded and land use approved; financing closing and construction start not confirmed
status.detail: City Council approved the site plan and 1041 review on 2025-04-03 and a total city package of about $3.8M on 2025-12-04, when the developer said closing could come within 60 days. The state selected the project for a $1.3M Proposition 123 concessionary loan in March-April 2026. In October 2026 the Aspen Daily News reported the project still working toward breaking ground, with a three-parcel plat only preliminarily approved by the planning commission.

next_step: Watch for Glenwood Springs City Council action on the Canyon Vista plat, a CHFA bond closing and a building permit.

key_numbers.meaning: 4 studios, 21 one-bedroom, 52 two-bedroom and 3 three-bedroom units at 20% to 80% AMI; half the units at or below 50% AMI; eight project-based vouchers.
About $21.3M over 10 years, plus $1,800,000 of accelerated state credit.

CHFA is the issuer; Garfield County voted 2-1 in July 2024 to give $3.9M of its 2024 bond cap. The application planned privately placed bonds paid down to $9.9M permanent and a $7.1M taxable construction loan.

key_numbers.value: About $3.8M of city money plus $1.3M Prop 123
key_numbers.meaning: Glenwood Springs 2C Workforce Housing Fund forgivable loan, fee backfill and an added $785,000; plus a preliminary $1.3M Proposition 123 concessionary loan.

facts.value: 51993 Highway 6, Glenwood Springs 81601, between U.S. Highway 6 and Donegan Road in West Glenwood, between the Elks Lodge and Six Canyon Apartments; nearly four acres
Applied as Glenwood Gardens; city approvals and later funding use the name Canyon Vista Apartments

Former Glenwood Gardens plant nursery with a few aging homes and a historic 1903 greenhouse first built at Redstone Castle for John Cleveland Osgood; a nonprofit is raising money to dismantle and save it

Two residential buildings approaching 40 feet, all units elevator-served, 138 parking spaces, storage unit with every home, rooftop deck, solar array on terraced retaining walls, relocated RFTA bus stop
All-electric, Energy Star, solar array sized for about 80% of electric baseload, per the application

Major Site/Architectural Plan (Planning File 01-25) and 1041 review (Planning File 05-25): Planning and Zoning Commission 2025-03-25; City Council approved both unanimously 2025-04-03 with seven design flexibility allowances for income-restricted housing
40-year covenant, per developers at the April 2025 council hearing
Examples given to council range from about $358 a month for a 20% AMI studio to about $2,130 for an 80% AMI three-bedroom
West Mountain Regional Health Alliance resident services, funded in the operating budget
Difficult Development Area; non-metro county priority under the QAP

money.source: Colorado accelerated state housing tax credit

money.note: CHFA is the conduit issuer; privately placed direct-purchase bonds sized at 55% of basis, paid down to $9.9M permanent, with a $7.1M taxable construction loan, per the application. Garfield County commissioners voted 2-1 to allocate $3.9M of the county's 2024 cap.

money.source: City of Glenwood Springs 2C Workforce Housing Fund
money.note: Forgivable loan approved July 2024 (forgiven over 15 years if workforce occupancy targets are met; target raised from 20 to 40 units), $730,640 fee backfill approved 2025-09-04 (5-2), and an added $785,000 approved 2025-12-04 (7-0), released in construction tranches and secured by a subordinate deed of trust. The 2024 application cited $1.57M of approved Prop 2C funds.

money.source: Proposition 123 Concessionary Debt (Affordable Housing Financing Fund)
money.note: LIHTC gap finance loan, FY25-26 Round One selection dated 2026-03-24; preliminary until the project's financial review.
Garfield County Housing Authority, which also offered to be special limited partner.

The application named subordinate loans from Impact Development Fund and the Colorado Clean Energy Fund and solar and 45L credits; in December 2025 the developer also cited added state housing dollars and a Colorado Health Foundation contribution. No amounts were found.

parties.name: Garfield County Housing Authority (vouchers; offered special limited partnership)

background.text: Cohen-Esrey has worked on the site since October 2022. The 2023 Round Two application proposed 131 units with 20 vouchers and $36.4M of bonds; it was not funded (inferred from the 2024 reapplication), and the 2024 version was cut to 80 units with as-of-right zoning and no variance requests.

In July 2024 Garfield County commissioners voted 2-1 to give $3.9M of county bond cap; Commissioner John Martin opposed, citing density and displacement of the gardens in West Glenwood. The project was then estimated at about $46 million.

At the April 2025 hearing, residents tied to the Mitchell Creek water district urged delay over a 1985 agreement on city water service inside the district; the application says the developer secured water rights that removed over $500,000 in tap and water fees.
Use of federal funds triggered a Section 106 historic review; the city Historic Preservation Commission was told on 2025-07-07 it would get review materials.
In September 2025 the developer reported a funding gap of about $3 million after expected federal sustainability money changed; the application had expected Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund eligibility.
The application targeted a summer 2025 groundbreaking; in April 2025 developers expected September 2025 and an 18-month build; in December 2025 they projected lease-up in 2027.
The market study cites a 12.2% capture rate under CHFA's method and zero vacancies at LIHTC and subsidized properties in the market area.

discrepancies.text: CHFA's award description lists 3 three-bedroom units out of 80, while the Post Independent reported in July 2024 that 55 of the 80 units would be three-bedroom.
The Post Independent and the application describe two residential buildings, while the Aspen Daily News describes three new buildings.
CHFA's award lists $25,130,000 in bonds, while the Post Independent reported the project would need just over $20 million of bond capacity.
The application says Garfield County delegated its full 2024 bond allocation to the project, while the Post Independent reported $3.9 million of the county's 2024 allocation.

open_questions: Whether and when the CHFA bonds and tax credit equity closed; the developer projected a closing in early 2026 and no record was found.
Who owns the land and on what terms (purchase or option), and the land price.
Total development cost now, equity investor, bond purchaser and the final general contractor.
Whether Division of Housing or Colorado Health Foundation funds were formally awarded, and amounts.
